sections.h2: What closing costs does a Georgia seller pay?
sections.html:
The charge that the state itself sets for sellers is the real estate transfer tax. Everything else on a Georgia settlement statement, such as attorney fees, payoff of the existing loan and any agent commission, comes from your contract and your lender, so it varies by deal.

Four items come with official rules you can check ahead of time: the transfer tax, the PT-61 declaration that goes with the deed, the property tax for the year, and withholding if the seller lives outside Georgia. The sections below cover each one, and the table near the end lines them up.

Ask the closing attorney or title company for a draft settlement statement several days before the closing date. Compare each line with the contract, because Georgia lets buyer and seller agree to move some of these charges.

sections.h2: How much is the Georgia real estate transfer tax?
sections.html:
The Department of Revenue prints the rate as $1 for the first $1,000 or fractional part of $1,000, plus 10 cents for each additional $100 or fractional part of $100, based on the sale price. The authority is O.C.G.A. 48-6-1 through 48-6-10.

The tax must be paid by the person who executes the deed or the person for whose benefit it is executed, and the Department says the seller is liable. It adds that parties frequently agree in the sales contract that the buyer will pay. If your contract is silent, the statute puts the cost on you, so read that clause before you sign.

The tax is an excise tax on the transfer of title, which the Georgia Superior Court Clerks' Cooperative Authority notes is not a property tax. Paying it does not settle your yearly property bill.

sections.h2: What is the PT-61 and who files it?
sections.html:
The PT-61 is the real estate transfer tax declaration, and one form is filed for each applicable deed. It is completed online through the Georgia Superior Court Clerks' Cooperative Authority's PT-61 eFiling portal, then a printed copy goes to the Clerk of Superior Court with the deed documents.

The deed cannot be recorded until the transfer tax is paid. When it is, the clerk or a deputy attaches a certification of payment. Your closing attorney normally prepares the PT-61 from the settlement figures, so your task is to supply accurate sale and parcel information.

For help with the electronic procedure, the Department of Revenue lists the Authority's customer support at (800) 304-5174 or locally at (404) 327-9760. For questions about taxability or an exemption, the Department directs you to the Clerk of Superior Court in the county where the property sits.

sections.h2: How are property taxes handled when you sell in Georgia?
sections.html:
Whoever owned the property on January 1 is responsible for that year's bill. The Department says that holds even if the sale happens on January 2, and that Georgia law does not allow a refund of taxes to partial-year owners.

Any sharing of that year's bill between you and the buyer is set by the contract. Taxes are normally due December 20 in most counties, though some counties choose another date, and taxpayers get 60 days from the billing date to pay. Fulton County, for one, set October 15 as the due date for most 2026 bills, with the City of Atlanta due September 30.

Use these steps before closing:

  • Ask the county tax commissioner whether the current bill is paid, partly paid or still to come.
  • Ask the closing attorney how the contract splits the year between you and the buyer.
  • Confirm that no county tax lien is filed with the clerk on the general execution docket, since the Department says county tax liens are handled there.

sections.h2: What is the intangible recording tax, and is it a seller cost?
sections.html:
The intangible recording tax applies to a new long-term note secured by real estate, so it is tied to the buyer's financing. The Department sets it at $1.50 for each $500 or fractional part of the note's face amount, with a $25,000 maximum on any single note.

The lender must record the security instrument within 90 days, and the holder of the note can pass the tax on to the borrower. The buyer's lender is the party that records the new security instrument. The Clerk of Superior Court collects the tax in most counties, with a short list of smaller counties where the tax commissioner or tax collector does.

sections.h2: What paperwork should a Georgia seller keep after closing?
sections.html:
Keep the final settlement statement, the recorded deed information, and any withholding statement the buyer gives you. If you are a nonresident, the Department says the buyer must give you a copy of the withholding return or equivalent document, and you attach it to your Georgia income tax return to claim the credit.

The IRS notes that if you receive a Form 1099-S, Proceeds From Real Estate Transactions, you must report the sale even when the gain is excludable. The settlement statement is the document you will use to check the figures on that form.

  • Final settlement statement showing the sale price, payoff and every charge.
  • Copy of the PT-61 and the clerk's certification that the transfer tax was paid, if your closing attorney provides them.
  • Property tax bill and proof of payment for the year of sale.
  • Any Form G-2RP or similar statement of Georgia tax withheld.

sections.h2: Does withholding apply when the seller lives outside Georgia?
sections.html:
It can. O.C.G.A. 48-7-128 requires the buyer to withhold 3% of the purchase price from a nonresident seller, or 3% of the gain if the seller provides a sworn gain affidavit. The buyer files and remits by the last day of the month after the closing month.

The Department lists exemptions, including a principal residence under the federal rules, a purchase price under $20,000, and a transfer to a mortgagee in foreclosure with no added consideration. An exemption certificate, Form IT-AFF3, is optional but helps the closing file. The Department's own FAQ describes it as income tax withholding.

faqs.q: Who pays the transfer tax in Georgia?
faqs.a: The seller is liable under the Department of Revenue's description, but buyer and seller often agree in the contract that the buyer pays. Check the contract language, since a silent contract leaves the cost with the seller.

faqs.q: What is the Georgia transfer tax rate?
faqs.a: The rate is $1 for the first $1,000 or fractional part, plus 10 cents for each additional $100 or fractional part, based on the sale price. The statutes are O.C.G.A. 48-6-1 through 48-6-10. Ask your closing attorney for the figure on your own settlement statement.

faqs.q: Can I get a property tax refund if I sell mid-year in Georgia?
faqs.a: No. The Department of Revenue says the owner on January 1 is responsible for the whole year, and that Georgia law does not allow a refund for partial-year owners. Sharing the bill between you and the buyer is a matter for the contract.

faqs.q: Who files the PT-61 in Georgia?
faqs.a: The filer completes it online through the clerks' authority portal, and one form is filed per applicable deed. Ask your closing attorney or title company to confirm who is preparing it and that it goes to the clerk with the deed.

faqs.q: Where do I ask about a transfer tax exemption?
faqs.a: Ask the Clerk of Superior Court in the county where the property is located. The Department of Revenue directs questions about taxability and exemptions there, and the clerk also certifies that the tax has been paid before the deed is recorded.
